cards.title: Product-first brand thesis: solve one problem before anything else
cards.summary: True Classic built $200M+ by nailing a single product problem (t-shirt fit) before expanding, then adding price and comfort as secondary pillars.
cards.use_when: Deciding what your hero product should be and what problem it solves before you build a catalog or run acquisition.
steps: Pick one problem the market is 'egregious' on — for True Classic it was fit. Founder Ryan Bartlett deliberately did not try to solve everything at once.
Find a partner with domain expertise you lack (Bartlett had no apparel background, so he partnered with co-founder Nick who did), and iterate samples until the core problem is solved.
Layer secondary pillars after fit: for True Classic these were price (bring 'premium to the masses' vs. overpriced incumbents) and comfort.
Keep product as the pillar above marketing. Bartlett: 'People think it's mostly marketing, but it's not. The product really stands on its own, and it kind of has to to get to these levels.'

Note the early demand signal: True Classic started with one t-shirt in six colors, did $20k month one and $15M year one — but Bartlett attributes the early fire to the product, not the ads, which he calls 'very average' and 'very traditional'.
caveats: This is one brand's experience, not a guarantee that a single hero product will scale. Bartlett repeatedly frames the outcome as founder belief and risk tolerance, not a replicable formula.
The early Facebook performance (pre-iOS 14) is explicitly described by Bartlett as a different world; do not treat that traffic dynamic as current.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Work backward from what is already selling in your category
cards.summary: Reverse-engineer winning products by studying Amazon review volume and category best-sellers, then solve price after the product is best-in-class.
cards.use_when: Selecting or designing a new product or SKU in a category where you have no internal data yet.
steps: Before designing, study the market: 'look on Amazon, look at what everyone's buying, look at the volume of reviews and work backwards from that.' Review volume is a proxy for units moved.
Identify which price points and which product types are already working — Bartlett calls the data 'all there' whereas historically you had to guess.
Build the product to be the absolute best you can on fit, comfort, durability, quality control, and wash/wear longevity first.
Solve for price second, based on your specific customer ('not really the market'), not by reverse-engineering margin from a target MSRP.
Do not begin from a target price and architect down; that is the opposite of True Classic's approach.
caveats: Amazon review volume is a category-demand signal, not a validated demand forecast for your brand.
Bartlett notes his own start was 'not that thoughtful' — he built something he loved and hoped others would. The reverse-engineering method is what he describes using at scale afterward.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Finance inventory growth with supplier net terms instead of outside capital
cards.summary: Fund large inventory buys by proving sales velocity to vendors and negotiating 60–90 day terms plus safety stock, rather than raising equity.
cards.use_when: Planning a large inventory buy or replenishment cycle and weighing vendor terms against raising capital.
steps: Prove sales first, then leverage that proof with vendors: True Classic started at $1M in credit, ramped to $5M, then $25M as sales grew — each tier opened more supplier float.
Lead with the relationship pitch: 'We're young, we're hungry, we're scrappy, we're going to grow this thing. Work with us.' Ask for 60–90 day terms or credit to float production.
Negotiate interest payments, extended net terms, and safety stock as levers if demand slows.
Use safety stock correctly: it is raw fabric purchased and held before it is cut and sewn, so a sellout can be turned quickly. This is inventory held for upside, not finished goods.
Plan the downside before you buy. True Classic's team explicitly gamed out 'vendors are going to come knocking — here is exactly what we'll say' before committing to a $40M inventory buy in year two.
caveats: Bartlett calls the $40M year-two buy 'out of our minds' — the team had no rigorous model other than forecast plus hope. Do not treat this as a recommended method of sizing an inventory bet.
$40M inventory via net terms is an example from one company, not a benchmark. Terms available to you depend on your scale and vendor relationships.
The founders also maxed out a couple hundred thousand in personal credit card debt early on — presented as a fact of their path, not advice.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Test many openers per ad creative, then scale the winner
cards.summary: Every True Classic ad carries 4–6 different openers because the first 3 seconds determine thumb-stop rate; test hooks cheap, then put budget behind the winner.
cards.use_when: Producing paid social video or static ads and trying to improve ad performance or cut creative-production waste.
steps: Build 4–6 alternate openers for each single piece of creative — their dodgeball parody shipped with about six.
Rationale: 'What we think is funny may not resonate with the customer.' Give the platform options to test into rather than betting on your taste.
Run a small budget behind each opener version, observe which hooks perform, then 'put Rocket Fuel behind that' — the winner gets the budget.
Iterate on winners already inside your own content rather than constantly making net-new concepts from scratch.
Front-load the opener because 'if you can't get them in the first 3 seconds, they're going to miss the greatness of the ad' — the opener is treated as the whole ballgame for thumb-stop rate.
caveats: This is a media-buying heuristic from one brand's ad account, not a validated lift benchmark.
The source describes testing openers, not a formal statistical test design — it is iterative media buying, so treat results as directional.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Build creative in three recurring buckets: value prop, comedy, DR/UGC
cards.summary: True Classic organizes paid creative into three repeatable buckets — visual side-by-side value prop, comedy/parody, and straight direct-response UGC — and reuses winners across categories.
cards.use_when: Setting up an evergreen creative pipeline or a content calendar for paid acquisition.
steps: Bucket 1 — Value prop / side-by-side: visually show your product next to the inferior incumbent so the difference is undeniable. Bartlett built these specifically to show why the shirt is different. They crushed on ROAS, so he repeated them.
Extend winning formats across categories: 'that's working really good for t-shirts — why don't we do that with underwear? Why don't we do that with denim?' Do side-by-sides everywhere.
Bucket 2 — Comedy / parody: nostalgic formats people recognize, rewritten with your brand's vibe. Worth testing aggressively, but only roll it out where it lands.
Bucket 3 — Straight DR/UGC: in-your-face direct response selling. Bartlett says all three buckets 'work on some level.'
Repurpose across funnel: put the side-by-side into collection pages and PDPs so the market-vs-you comparison does merchandising work after the click, not just in the ad.
caveats: Bartlett notes the ideal funnel ('brand first, DR later') is not fully controllable: 'the ads just show to whoever, whenever,' so the sequencing is a desired state, not a guarantee.
Comedy sometimes misses — he pulls egregious ads quickly and reverts. Expect misses and build the ability to cut them.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Treat creative as an open, company-wide idea channel
cards.summary: A company-wide #ideas Slack channel where anyone including interns can submit creative or product ideas, with leadership free to escalate or kill them, feeds the brand's best content.
cards.use_when: Sourcing ad creative and product concepts when you want more variety than your marketing team can generate alone.
steps: Create one open channel that the entire company can post to — any idea, any type: video creative, product ideas, or anything else.
Deliberately invite ideas from the most junior people: Bartlett says 'you could be Mr. intern just started yesterday and come up with one of the best ideas in the company.'
Give creative leads autonomy to take big risks. Bartlett's stated strength is letting them do whatever they want and 'letting the chips fall where they may,' then deciding after the fact.
Fast-kill misses without drama: if something is too over-the-top or doesn't land, pull it and revert to what works.

Escalate winners hard. Example: a social team member proposed paying off teachers' wish lists at back-to-school — it went viral, reached news stations, and the spend scaled from roughly $5k to a couple hundred thousand because Bartlett reacted to the moment as demand snowballed.
caveats: The teachers-wish-list outcome is a single viral example, not a repeatable forecasting method. Bartlett himself says it started tiny and only snowballed because of timing and reaction.
Open idea channels need explicit kill criteria from leadership, or risk-tolerance turns into unmanaged spend.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Shift media spend from DR toward brand by widening your attribution window
cards.summary: True Classic is testing a deliberate pivot away from day-1 direct response toward brand-oriented spend, accepting short-term attribution loss to look at longer-window ROAS.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to split paid budget between direct-response retargeting and top-of-funnel brand or comedy content.
steps: Make brand the first brand interaction by putting more spend into brand content and keeping DR units mostly for retargeting.
Judge brand spend beyond day-one ROAS: 'if you just open up the attribution window a little bit and look beyond day one ROROWAZ, it opens up a new world for you.'
Accept the short-term loss: Bartlett acknowledges 'it's scary' and the whole team is 'a little freaked out,' but frames it as a bet on long-term compounding.
Set the fallback upfront: worst case, move back to what has worked. This makes the experiment bounded.

Bet on the post-click experience to carry conversion: 'I don't need the ad to convert them necessarily... let me just make them laugh, create an emotional connection, and let them figure it out when they get to the website' — with CRO, side-by-sides, and cart upsells doing conversion work.
caveats: Bartlett explicitly says 'we'll see how it pans out' — this is an in-progress experiment, not proven lift.
Brand spend leading to delayed conversion relies on a strong on-site experience; without CRO and merchandising it may not pay back.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Validate ad spend with post-purchase surveys, not platform attribution alone
cards.summary: True Classic uses post-purchase survey data (where did you find us) as the primary read on media mix, layered on top of Triple Whale, Northbeam, and agency tools.
cards.use_when: Assessing whether paid channels are driving real incremental revenue, especially after a data-privacy change breaks native attribution.
steps: Run a post-purchase survey asking where people found you, and track the word-of-mouth segment over time.

Treat that segment's trend as your organic health signal: 'you watch that word of mouth segment continue to increase and increase and increase over time, that means you're doing the right thing organically to push you past paid media.'
Do not rely on a single source. True Classic stacks Triple Whale (current), previously Northbeam, plus agency-side internal tools.

Use the surveys specifically to sanity-check channel allocation when native attribution is unreliable — the source notes Meta lost micro-data post-iOS 14 and native reporting became 'pissing in the wind.'
caveats: Post-purchase survey is self-reported and can undercount or overcount channels; use it as a directional read alongside platform tools, not a single truth source.
This is a described practice, not a validated model for the true incremental contribution of a channel.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Use post-purchase upsells on already-authorized cards to lift AOV
cards.summary: True Classic's cart architecture uses multi-tier gift-with-purchase thresholds to force AOV up and cross-pollinate categories, then layers post-purchase upsells on already-authorized cards.
cards.use_when: Designing cart or checkout flows to increase average order value and cross-sell between categories without hurting purchase conversion.
steps: Layer multi-tier gift-with-purchase thresholds into cart to do two jobs: force AOV up and cross-pollinate product categories in one order.
Configure the thresholds so each tier introduces a different category you want customers to try, not just a deeper discount of the same item.
Add a post-purchase upsell step after the transaction completes — because the card is already authorized, this is a separate consented transaction that does not interrupt the primary purchase flow.
Match a gift-with-purchase ladder to your existing margin structure so each threshold still contributes profit; the source frames this as EBITDA-positive, not a pure promo.
Instrument the cart and checkout to measure AOV lift from tiers and AOV lift from post-purchase upsells separately, so you know which lever is contributing.
caveats: This is a stated description of True Classic's architecture, not measured lift numbers; test your own thresholds.
Aggressive gift thresholds can erode margin; do not assume cross-sell AOV lift offsets a giveaway you've priced poorly.
Support depends on your cart/checkout platform's post-purchase feature set, so verify current capability before designing around it.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Lean into giving to arbitrage CAC over the long term
cards.summary: Bartlett treats giving product as the highest form of marketing — free products that get worn publicly create word-of-mouth, referrals, and rising post-purchase word-of-mouth share that eventually offsets paid CAC.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run free-product sampling, gifting, or philanthropy as an acquisition and retention lever.
steps: Only run this if you genuinely believe in the product: 'if you believe in your product, you should be able to give it to somebody, and if they love it, they're going to buy it later.'
Design small, unique giveaways people can pass along — the 'poker chip' with a custom code lets a stranger redeem for your product and creates a personal moment.
Prioritize recipients you will actually see again (delivery drivers, service workers, local businesses) so you observe the full loop: giver gives, receiver returns wearing the product.
Track the second-order effect in post-purchase surveys: word-of-mouth share should rise over time if giving is working.
Be genuine about why you are doing it. Bartlett is explicit that giving must be 'because it's the right thing to do for people,' not just to 'arbitrage CAC.'
caveats: The poker chip and teacher wish list are anecdotes, not measured CAC arbitrage; results depend on product and audience.
Bartlett only recommends this at companies with deep product belief and margin room — giving product costs real money and only pays back if retention and referral are real.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Build a 'wow budget' to win back upset customers and reward high-LTV buyers
cards.summary: Use a fixed weekly budget to reverse angry customers and surprise high-LTV buyers with gifts outside your product line to manufacture word-of-mouth moments that no one else is doing.
cards.use_when: Building a retention or customer-experience program that converts service recovery and VIP recognition into referral and LTV.
steps: Set a fixed weekly dollar amount for the wow budget — the partner brand on this podcast says it created one starting January 1st after hearing Bartlett describe the practice.
Two use cases: (a) save angry customers who felt strongly enough to escalate, and (b) reward high-LTV customers pulled from your CRM.
Give gifts outside your own product line. Bartlett's team, handling an escalated customer, sends something that ISN'T True Classic as a deliberate surprise.
Make the service recovery personal and overboard, not scripted: 'He's going to go overboard and really make a moment out of it.'
Assume the payoff is word-of-mouth, not direct revenue: the upset customer becomes a story-teller in rooms full of potential customers.
caveats: The source frames wow budget as a long-horizon brand investment, not a measurable short-term ROI play. Bartlett: 'you will be so pleasantly surprised at what happens when you deploy that on the world.'
Reverse the aggressive tone of the story: the payoff assumes you send something significant, not a token coupon.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Run service recovery out of your own house before you trust AI with the whole conversation
cards.summary: True Classic uses AI to route and bucket support queries to the right human, but refuses to let AI handle the conversation end-to-end because the human moment is the differentiator most companies skip.
cards.use_when: Choosing or configuring a customer service stack, or setting escalation rules for AI-assisted support.
steps: Pick AI-first support software that can do the early legwork — bucketing the query to get the customer in front of the right rep.
Explicitly limit AI to routing: 'it's not the AI agent going and handling your entire situation... the AI is just really good at who's the best fit on the team to deal with this type of person.'
Match the rep to the query type — product, shipping, or other specialty — so the person who owns the issue handles it.

Keep the channel human when the stakes are high: 'we don't have to love our own product, but the people we're selling to have to absolutely love it,' and if something goes wrong 'you better show up for them or you don't deserve to keep them as a customer.'

Hire the best possible CX people rather than the cheapest. Bartlett says the belief that overseas talent at a fraction of the price is 'better than domestic talent that is embedded' is 'a huge miss' — and admits his own company made it and is progressively moving CX back in-house and domestic.
caveats: The recommended tool stack is evolving quickly — Bartlett says they've been through multiple platforms (Gorgeousiq, now Zai) and are 'always looking to see who's innovating,' so verify the current interface and capabilities before committing.
This is one founder's opinion on offshoring CX, not a universal rule; framing it as 'people are not stupid' is his read, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Index the customer by scaling the unscalable pre- and post- purchase moments
cards.summary: Bartlett's core thesis is customer obsession: over-extend on obvious gestures — calling every $1k+ buyer, wow gifts, service recovery — because almost no competitor does it, so the ROI compounds through word-of-mouth.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest in service and experience levers that don't show up as direct attributed revenue.
steps: Identify the moments most competitors skip: pre-purchase high-intent attention, wow gifts, and recovery after a failure.

Do the unscalable work at the scale you can handle. Bartlett called every customer spending over $1,000 every Friday for a period — on the explicit theory that inputs and outputs are worth watching but don't always show direct attribution.

Benchmark against 50% effort: Bartlett claims most companies do 'a 50% job' on customer experience and that even a 75% version corners the market — so a genuine over-delivery is enough to differentiate.
Run the loop: the biggest source of new demand at this stage is word-of-mouth from these moments, which shows up in post-purchase survey as a rising segment over time.
Use the 'look good, feel good, do good' frame to decide which experiences get funded — if a moment makes someone feel better about themselves and comes from genuine belief, it's on-brand.
caveats: The 50% and 75% figures are the source's rhetorical estimates, not measured market data.
This compounding depends on product quality; if the product can't deliver, no amount of service magic preserves LTV.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Bias toward high risk tolerance and simulate the downside before making the big bet
cards.summary: Bartlett's poker background produced a founder-level willingness to bet big on inventory and brand — but each big bet is paired with an explicit downside scenario and negotiation plan.
cards.use_when: Making a large commitment — a big inventory buy, a brand campaign, a supplier contract — where the wrong call could materially hurt the business.
steps: First, build personal tolerance for losing: 'when you can take big bets on yourself and not be afraid to lose because you're just used to losing... you get numb to that feeling.'

Before committing, write down the downside in plain terms: True Classic's team asked, 'what are we going to say to them when they come knocking,' and rehearsed the answer — ask for terms, interest, safety stock, whatever leeway the vendor can give.

Make the bet on your own conviction, not on a perfect model. Bartlett describes the $40M inventory call as 'a bunch of knuckleheads sitting around a table' agreeing on a number based on forecast they hoped they'd hit.
When the downside actually happens, negotiate from loyalty framing: 'are you with us or are you not? ... you can be our partner and we'll give you all the business.'
caveats: This is a high-variance strategy that worked for True Classic; the same approach can produce a loss if the forecast misses and vendors will not extend terms.
Bartlett calls the $40M year-two inventory bet 'out of our minds.' Do not treat that number as a formula.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: EOS and operating cadence: adopt systems only once the team stabilizes
cards.summary: True Classic ran with 12 scrappy generalists 'hanging on for dear life' for years, only adopting EOS in roughly the last year — implying that a formal operating system was not what built the early velocity.
cards.use_when: Deciding when to install a formal operating system like EOS, or whether your current growth speed warrants one yet.
steps: At the small-team stage, prioritize hiring generalists ('entrepreneurial DNA,' Swiss Army knife profiles) who can cover multiple functions at once — one ops generalist covered platforms, Netsuite integrations, and the job of ten people later hired for separately.
Delay formal operating systems until you have the team, processes, and scale to internalize them. Bartlett says True Classic didn't start EOS until about a year before the interview.
As you pass the early stage, layer EOS on top of existing all-hands and touchpoints rather than replacing them.
Expect that the operating system reveals gaps, not that it fixes velocity by itself.
caveats: The source does not name specific EOS outcomes — do not treat EOS as a causal driver of True Classic's revenue.
The early-stage 'just run and gun' approach is described as a tradeoff; it left them with growth they may have missed by not hiring more people sooner.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Use a Slack kudos app with decaying coins tied to core values
cards.summary: True Classic gives each employee a weekly budget of coins that expire if unused, tied to specific company core values, redeemable for real money — creating peer-to-peer recognition and amplifying culture.
cards.use_when: Building peer recognition and retention mechanisms in a fast-scaling team, especially when most of the team is remote or dispersed.
steps: Deploy a Slack-based recognition tool (Bartlett refers to a 'Kudos app'). Give each employee a fixed number of coins each week.
Make coins expire: 'if you don't use them, they go away. So you're forced to give.' This is the mechanism that keeps recognition flowing.
Require the coin-giver to select which core value the recipient exemplified and add a short message explaining why — not just 'hey, you did this.'
Set the exchange rate (e.g., roughly a dollar per coin) and let recipients convert coins to cash or gift cards from Amazon, Starbucks, Uber Eats, or similar.
Budget it as a fixed P&L line — essentially a set dollar pool per week divided into coins distributed across the company.
Let peers, not just leadership, award coins: 'it's not just us leadership rewarding the people — the people are rewarding the people.'
caveats: The efficacy is Bartlett's anecdotal report ('one of the best moves that we made early on'), not a controlled measurement.
Requires a Slack-centered culture; if your team is not in Slack, the mechanism will not reach them.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Hiring for A-players: homework assignments, personality screening, and long-runway process
cards.summary: True Classic uses a 4–6 week pipeline including a role-relevant homework assignment presented live, plus a personality test, weighting grit and generalist ability over credentials.
cards.use_when: Hiring for a role on a fast-scaling ecommerce team where the wrong hire is costly, especially for roles where the company will outgrow the person in 12–24 months.
steps: Assign a real, role-specific deliverable as 'homework.' Example: for a head of product, ask 'what does the 2026 roadmap look like given what you've seen with True Classic?' Expect month-one, month-two specifics and things the company hasn't done enough of.
Require them to present it live. Evaluate intentionality and granularity — 'not just here's what Abercrombie's doing, you guys should do that.'
Screen for grit via background signals: veterans (military), competitive athletes, and self-reliant individuals (the source cites wrestlers making weight as a self-reliance marker).
Apply a personality test to check fit with the team's known good and bad profiles.

Do not hire for potential 1–2 years out. Bartlett says it is 'very dangerous' because less than about 5% of people evolve as fast as a hyper-growth business — the people you start with are not the people you end with.

Accept the 4–6 week hiring runway so the process screens out low-effort applicants. Bartlett notes hiring managers sometimes fall in love with a candidate before homework, then reverse course after seeing shallow work.
caveats: The 'less than 5%' figure is Bartlett's estimate, not a measured statistic.
The homework method has a known weakness — strong candidates over-perform on homework and may not reflect day-to-day performance; Bartlett names this tradeoff himself.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Use founder visibility and content to attract A+ hires
cards.summary: Bartlett attributes a meaningful part of True Classic's ability to attract top talent (with ~60 employees at >$200M+ revenue) to podcast clips and LinkedIn content that let candidates preview how the company thinks and operates.
cards.use_when: Recruiting senior talent to a growing ecommerce brand when you cannot outspend incumbents on compensation.
steps: Publish short clips and long-form content where leaders discuss how they think about product, customers, and the business.
Distribute on LinkedIn where the professional audience sees it in-feed and can reach out about roles.

Use the content as a pre-hire culture test: 'it gives people a really good insight to how we think, how we operate, how we deal with employees' — candidates self-select in or out before the process starts.
Pair with persistent pursuing of specific hires. Bartlett first hired his eventual CMO Ben as a $500/month Meta consultant, then grew the relationship across years until the company could afford him.
caveats: Bartlett explicitly notes you have to be able to afford senior A+ hires — this technique opens the door but does not replace compensation.
The ~$3M per employee figure cited by the interviewer is a revenue-per-head ratio, not a compensation benchmark or hiring target.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx

cards.title: Run all-hands customer calls to install customer obsession as a north star
cards.summary: True Classic regularly puts the whole company on calls with real customers to hear how the brand has affected their lives — with service and product quality made the top operating priority over marketing perception.
cards.use_when: Reinforcing customer-centric behavior across a scaling team when teammates drift from the customer's actual experience.
steps: Schedule all-hands customer calls where the entire company listens to a real customer describe their experience — good or bad.
Push past fit and shipping logistics to the bigger story: 'it's not just about it fitting a little bit better, it's about the bigger picture of what the brand has been able to do for their life.'
Use those calls to remind the team why the work matters so it functions as a north star.
Follow it with continuous manager touchpoints asking for feedback ('how is this going for you? anything I can do better for you?').
Bartlett's own stated priority for the company is 'unequivocally at the top the word customer obsession' — not marketing.
caveats: Bartlett admits True Classic is 'not enough' on formal team culture-building beyond these touchpoints — the all-hands customer call is one of the few structural practices.
This is not a substitute for process investment; it is a belief-alignment mechanism.
cards.source_name: This Is How a T-Shirt Brand Outsmarted the Entire Industry.docx
